text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Consent first: every examination, test, and treatment is explained and offered, and he may decline any of it; intimate examinations only with his agreement at each step and with a chaperone offered. The estrogen he was given as a condition of avoiding prison was not freely consented treatment, and no further doses will be given
  • Gynecomastia workup: breast and testicular examination; testosterone, estradiol, LH, FSH, prolactin, SHBG, hCG, AFP, liver, kidney, and thyroid tests today; scrotal ultrasound; breast ultrasound only if the examination becomes equivocal
  • Endocrinology consultation to confirm that the estrogen explains the findings and to advise on recovery of the gonadal axis, testosterone therapy, bone health, and surgery
  • Watchful waiting for the gynecomastia after the estrogen stops; testosterone, estradiol, LH, and FSH every six to eight weeks until normal; no testosterone therapy while the axis is recovering; a surgical opinion if gynecomastia persists about twelve months and troubles him
  • Bone health: vitamin D replacement, calcium from food, continued running and strength work; bone density scan only if hypogonadism persists beyond six months or a fracture occurs
  • Weekly psychotherapy with a gay-affirming clinic psychologist for about 16 sessions, addressing the prosecution, the coerced treatment, and minority stress; an antidepressant offered and declined for now, to be reconsidered if the PHQ-9 has not fallen by half at about eight weeks
  • Collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping steps, people to contact, the clinic number, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; suicide-risk review and PHQ-9 at every visit
  • Sexual health as routine adult care: HIV and STI testing and a PrEP discussion offered at his preventive visit, with his consent; libido and erectile function reviewed as testosterone recovers
  • Affirming practice: his orientation, name, and pronouns recorded as he chooses; his records shared only with his consent; a written letter from this clinic, at his request, confirming that the estrogen he was given was not medically indicated
  • Add bupropion XL 150 mg each morning, chosen by him after an informed discussion of options and side effects; nurse telephone check at two weeks; PHQ-9 and blood pressure at each visit

resource.description: Recognize and manage the harm of high-dose estrogen given to a 40-year-old gay man without his free and informed consent: evaluate gynecomastia as the EAA 2019 guideline advises (history, breast and testicular examination, testosterone, estradiol, LH, FSH, prolactin, SHBG, hCG, AFP, liver, kidney, and thyroid tests, scrotal ultrasound, breast imaging only if the examination is equivocal), name the cause as iatrogenic, stop the exposure, monitor recovery of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis without testosterone therapy while it recovers, protect bone health, and offer surgery if gynecomastia persists; treat a moderate depressive episode with measurement-based care, gay-affirming psychotherapy, and an antidepressant only if he chooses one, with a structured suicide-risk assessment, a safety plan, and the 988 Lifeline; offer HIV and STI testing and a PrEP discussion as routine adult care with his consent; and practise LGBTQ-affirming primary care. Sexual orientation is recorded as part of his social history, never as a problem, and every test and treatment requires his free, informed consent.
